bull_bear.body:
- Prioritising early BESS deployment at existing substations to monetise spare transmission capacity.
- Disciplined capex deferral on solar modules where substations delayed (no penalty under CTU sync framework).
- Refinancing to lower interest cost; debt-covenant DSRA maintained.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Other income / DSRA optics:** INR157 cr "other income" is debt-funded interest with offsetting finance cost — quality of reported PAT lower than headline.
- **Merchant arbitrage durability:** ~75-80% margins assume INR6 arbitrage persists; mgmt guides 4-5 yrs of elevated peak prices (INR9-10 thermal peak), but admits "anybody's guess." As ~200-300 GWh national BESS builds out, spread compresses.
- **Transmission/CTU delays:** ~6-month typical delay; only ~60% substations on time; revenue timing risk (mitigated by BESS preponement).
- **Curtailment:** small (~INR5-6 cr FY26 real curtailment); 2 Rajasthan state-grid projects exposed; rest CTU-protected.
- **Standalone BESS zero-date stuck** on NHPC trading-margin regulatory dispute.
- Supply-chain/geopolitical risk on battery cell imports.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: - Confident, granular, candid — quantified curtailment, named substation-by-substation timelines, openly flagged DSRA/other-income mechanics. CFO transition (Rajat Kumar Singh → Arun Chopra) handled smoothly. Strong command of regulatory nuance (MNRE/CERC/CTU/REIA). Tone bullish on BESS-led firming demand.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- The MNRE clarification (BESS charged from conventional power under FDRE can sell merchant without buyer NOC until RE commissions) is the single biggest revenue-preponement enabler — ACME is exploiting energised brownfield substations to run batteries years before PPA COD.
- "Plain vanilla solar is the hardest to sell"; states now demand at least 1-2 hrs peak power → industry capex per MW rising even as headline GW bids fall (FDRE carries 1.5-2x solar behind battery).
- Deferring module capex (just-in-time, 60% of cost) is a structural IRR lever the whole industry uses under the no-penalty CTU sync regime.
- DSO of 14 days for an Indian renewable IPP is exceptional and reflects deliberate 100%-central-offtake portfolio construction (consciously avoided C&I/state-grid).
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Fully integrated in-house EPC and O&M platform giving control over cost, timelines and quality and flexibility in choice of technology and suppliers
- Long-term contracted revenue: electricity sold to central and state government-backed off-takers under PPAs typically running 25 years
- One of the top 10 renewable energy Independent Power Producers in India, with one of India's largest commissioned BESS capacities at 3.6 GWh
- Land and connectivity secured ahead of execution — over 15,000 acres secured across 11 states and roughly 10 GW of connectivity inventory available for upcoming bids
- Disciplined bidding track record, with a 23.8% bid success ratio in FY 2026
- Operating reliability with a 25.9% capacity utilisation factor, 99.5% plant availability and 99.2% grid availability
- Geographically diversified pan-India portfolio across 11 states reducing regional resource risk
- Technology diversification across solar, wind, hybrid, FDRE and BESS, shifting the mix towards firm and dispatchable power
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Single-activity and single-sector concentration — 100% of turnover comes from a single activity — generation of power from renewable energy (NIC 351) — with no exports, so earnings are wholly exposed to Indian renewable generation economics with no diversifying business line.
- Off-taker concentration in government and government-backed counterparties — Power is sold almost entirely to central and state government-owned entities under long-term PPAs — SECI, NTPC, SJVN, NHPC and state DISCOMs — so receivables and cash flows depend on the payment discipline of a narrow set of state counterparties; the AR notes FY 2025 DSO excluded INR 490 million of outstanding dues from AP DISCOMs recovered only after an APERC ruling.
- Transmission infrastructure and grid connectivity constraints — Management states that transmission infrastructure and grid connectivity remain critical enablers, with limited connectivity availability expected until FY 2028-FY 2029, directly influencing project execution timelines and conversion of the pipeline into operating assets.
- Project execution risk on a large under-construction pipeline — With 5,088 MW under construction against 2,982 MW operational, most of the contracted portfolio is yet to be built; the forward-looking statement explicitly lists project execution and equipment supply among the uncertainties to which stated targets are subject.
- Financing availability and rising leverage — The build-out is debt-funded — net debt rose to INR 128,300 million in FY 2026 from INR 75,067 million, with net debt to net worth at 2.5x and debt to equity at 3.8x — and management identifies availability of financing as a stated risk factor; the Company runs against a self-imposed ceiling of under 5.5x Net Debt/Run-Rate EBITDA (3.9x at FY 2026).
- Regulatory and policy change, including ISTS waiver withdrawal and ALMM sourcing rules — Phased withdrawal of ISTS charge waivers raises applicable charges from 25% in FY 2026 to 50% in FY 2027, 75% in FY 2028 and 100% thereafter, altering inter-state project economics; separately, ALMM List-II applicability on three projects (SECI FDRE at INR 6/kWh, SJVN FDRE at INR 7/kWh and the REMCL RTC bids) constrains module and cell sourcing. Regulatory developments are named in the forward-looking statement as a risk to stated targets.
- Tariff compression and competitive bidding pressure — Discovered tariffs in FY 2026 GUVNL auctions reached INR 2.34/kWh and storage tariffs compressed 71% between 2023 and 2025 to INR 1.48 lakhs/MW/month; management notes that sub-economic pricing and financial closures for ultra-low bids create near-term execution adjustments, and the Company's bid success ratio was 23.8%, so growth depends on winning at economic prices.
- Weather, resource variability and climate exposure — Generation depends on solar irradiation and wind resource, and weather conditions are named in the forward-looking statement as a risk; the AR notes early rains and prolonged monsoons impacted national peak demand in Fiscal 2026, and the Company plans climate-risk screening across 100% of operating and under-construction sites only by FY 2029.
- High employee attrition — Turnover for permanent employees was 28.90% in FY 2025-26 (44.11% in FY 2024-25), a structurally elevated rate for a business whose in-house EPC and O&M model — expanded from five to seven project-led teams during the year — depends on retaining execution capability.
- Merchant exposure on commissioned battery storage — Commissioned BESS capacity is being advanced on a short-term merchant basis, leaving that portion of storage revenue exposed to market tariffs rather than contracted PPAs, although the majority of planned BESS capacity is linked to PPA-backed projects.

outlook.body: ACME Solar ended FY 2026 with an aggregate operational capacity of 2,982 MW, commissioned Battery Energy Storage Systems of 1,324 MWh and an under-construction pipeline of 5,088 MW, giving a total contracted portfolio of 8,070 MW including approximately 20 GWh of BESS across 11 states. During FY 2026 the Company executed 442 MW of renewable capacity and was awarded projects for 1,400 MW of peak-power FDRE capacity, taking total under-construction contracted capacity to 5,088 MW; cumulative FY26 PPA signed capacity stood at 3,288 MW plus 550 MWh of standalone BESS. Since 31st March 2026 the Company has, through its subsidiaries, commissioned a further 2,297 MWh of BESS, taking total operational BESS capacity to 3,621 MWh at the end of July 2026, and added 8 MW of wind capacity from the ACME Eco Clean Energy Private Limited wind project, taking operational portfolio capacity to 2,990 MW as of 31st July 2026; PPAs of 600 MW were signed over the same period, lifting the PPA-signed portfolio to 3,880 MW. Technology-wise the contracted portfolio comprises 3,140 MW of solar, 150 MW of installed wind and 4,780 MW of FDRE and hybrid projects, with about 20 GWh of BESS. The majority of planned BESS capacity is linked to PPA-backed projects and will be connected to operational or near-term temporary GNA-ready substations, mitigating transmission connectivity risk and enabling early monetisation of cash flows, while commissioned BESS is being run on a short-term merchant basis using the existing transmission infrastructure of operational projects. Land and connectivity are secured ahead of execution, with over 15,000 acres secured across 11 states (3,000+ additional acres acquired since 31st March 2026) and roughly 10 GW of connectivity inventory available for upcoming bids. Execution is expected to scale by an additional ~1.5 GW in FY 2027, with a stated target of a 10 GW operational renewable portfolio and 25 GWh of BESS by 2030. Milestones include a pilot 15 MW solar project in Gujarat in 2011, 1 GW installed by 2017 across 10 states, over 2 GW by 2018, 3 GW commissioned by 2022, 3,380 MW of hybrid and FDRE projects secured in 2023-24 alongside a 1,200 MW ISTS project commissioned in Rajasthan and a first 150 MW wind project awarded by GUVNL in Gujarat, and diversification into BESS with Indian Railways' first 130 MW Round-the-Clock renewable tender secured in 2025.

outlook.body:
- India's 500 GW non-fossil fuel target by 2030 driving long-term renewable investments; renewables were roughly 275 GW (52%) of installed capacity as of March 2026
- Widening intraday tariff differentials — daytime renewable generation can reduce tariffs to as low as INR 0.05 per unit while peak and night-time demand can command up to INR 10 per unit — significantly strengthening the commercial case for storage-backed renewable solutions
- Declining battery costs, now below USD 100/kWh, significantly improving the commercial viability of large-scale storage deployment and accelerating industry adoption
- Procurement shifting from standalone solar towards FDRE, hybrid and Round-the-Clock configurations, which typically require a minimum 40% CUF together with four-hour peak supply capability
- CRISIL Intelligence expects India's power sector to attract INR 37-42 trillion of investments during FY 2027-FY 2031, with a substantial share to renewable generation, transmission and distribution
- Transmission infrastructure and grid connectivity remain critical enablers, with limited connectivity availability expected until FY 2028-FY 2029, influencing project execution timelines and pipeline conversion
- Developers with integrated project development, EPC and O&M capabilities, diversified funding and disciplined capital allocation expected to be better positioned as procurement models move to integrated renewable-plus-storage solutions requiring larger upfront investment and stronger balance sheets
- Merchant storage opportunities supported by energy arbitrage
- Phased withdrawal of ISTS charge waivers is influencing inter-state renewable economics, with applicable charges rising from 25% in FY 2026 to 50% in FY 2027, 75% in FY 2028 and 100% thereafter; eligible projects delayed by transmission unavailability can retain the graded waiver
- ALMM List-II applicability is limited to three ACME projects (the SECI FDRE projects at INR 6/kWh, the SJVN FDRE projects at INR 7/kWh, and the REMCL RTC bids); remaining projects are exempt as their bids were submitted before 31st August 2025
- Total contracted renewable portfolio of 8,070 MW including approximately 20 GWh of BESS, comprising 2,982 MW operational (37%) and 5,088 MW under construction (63%)
- Cumulative FY26 PPA signed capacity of 3,288 MW plus 550 MWh standalone BESS; PPA signed portfolio rose to 3,880 MW as of 31st July 2026 after signing PPAs of 600 MW since 31st March 2026
- LOA awarded capacity of 1,800 MW
- Secured 1,400 MW of peak-power FDRE capacity during FY 2026
- Signed approximately 1.7 GW of PPAs during the year, strengthening long-term revenue visibility
- Ordered 10+ GWh of battery capacity, covering the entire under-construction PPA-signed portfolio as of 31st July 2026
- Roughly 10 GW of connectivity inventory available (secured and applied) for upcoming bids, with over 15,000 acres of land secured across 11 states
- Off-taker split of total portfolio: 84% state and other off-takers, 14% central off-takers, 2% GUVNL

risks.note: 100% of turnover comes from a single activity — generation of power from renewable energy (NIC 351) — with no exports, so earnings are wholly exposed to Indian renewable generation economics with no diversifying business line.

risks.risk: Off-taker concentration in government and government-backed counterparties
risks.note: Power is sold almost entirely to central and state government-owned entities under long-term PPAs — SECI, NTPC, SJVN, NHPC and state DISCOMs — so receivables and cash flows depend on the payment discipline of a narrow set of state counterparties; the AR notes FY 2025 DSO excluded INR 490 million of outstanding dues from AP DISCOMs recovered only after an APERC ruling.

risks.risk: Transmission infrastructure and grid connectivity constraints
risks.note: Management states that transmission infrastructure and grid connectivity remain critical enablers, with limited connectivity availability expected until FY 2028-FY 2029, directly influencing project execution timelines and conversion of the pipeline into operating assets.

risks.risk: Project execution risk on a large under-construction pipeline
risks.note: With 5,088 MW under construction against 2,982 MW operational, most of the contracted portfolio is yet to be built; the forward-looking statement explicitly lists project execution and equipment supply among the uncertainties to which stated targets are subject.

The build-out is debt-funded — net debt rose to INR 128,300 million in FY 2026 from INR 75,067 million, with net debt to net worth at 2.5x and debt to equity at 3.8x — and management identifies availability of financing as a stated risk factor; the Company runs against a self-imposed ceiling of under 5.5x Net Debt/Run-Rate EBITDA (3.9x at FY 2026).

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: The Company develops, constructs, owns, operates and maintains grid-connected renewable energy projects across India, spanning solar, wind, hybrid, Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) and standalone Battery Energy Storage Systems. Electricity generated is supplied primarily to central and state government entities and government-backed agencies, including SECI, NTPC, SJVN, NHPC and State Distribution Companies (DISCOMs), under long-term Power Purchase Agreements typically for 25 years. It has in-house engineering, procurement, construction and operation & maintenance capabilities, allowing it to control processes, costs and timelines and giving flexibility in the choice of technology and suppliers.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's 500 GW non-fossil fuel target by 2030 driving long-term renewable investments; renewables were roughly 275 GW (52%) of installed capacity as of March 2026
- Widening intraday tariff differentials — daytime renewable generation can reduce tariffs to as low as INR 0.05 per unit while peak and night-time demand can command up to INR 10 per unit — significantly strengthening the commercial case for storage-backed renewable solutions
- Declining battery costs, now below USD 100/kWh, significantly improving the commercial viability of large-scale storage deployment and accelerating industry adoption
- Procurement shifting from standalone solar towards FDRE, hybrid and Round-the-Clock configurations, which typically require a minimum 40% CUF together with four-hour peak supply capability
- CRISIL Intelligence expects India's power sector to attract INR 37-42 trillion of investments during FY 2027-FY 2031, with a substantial share to renewable generation, transmission and distribution
- Transmission infrastructure and grid connectivity remain critical enablers, with limited connectivity availability expected until FY 2028-FY 2029, influencing project execution timelines and pipeline conversion
- Developers with integrated project development, EPC and O&M capabilities, diversified funding and disciplined capital allocation expected to be better positioned as procurement models move to integrated renewable-plus-storage solutions requiring larger upfront investment and stronger balance sheets
- Merchant storage opportunities supported by energy arbitrage
- Phased withdrawal of ISTS charge waivers is influencing inter-state renewable economics, with applicable charges rising from 25% in FY 2026 to 50% in FY 2027, 75% in FY 2028 and 100% thereafter; eligible projects delayed by transmission unavailability can retain the graded waiver

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: ACME Solar ended FY 2026 with an aggregate operational capacity of 2,982 MW, commissioned Battery Energy Storage Systems of 1,324 MWh and an under-construction pipeline of 5,088 MW, giving a total contracted portfolio of 8,070 MW including approximately 20 GWh of BESS across 11 states. During FY 2026 the Company executed 442 MW of renewable capacity and was awarded projects for 1,400 MW of peak-power FDRE capacity, taking total under-construction contracted capacity to 5,088 MW; cumulative FY26 PPA signed capacity stood at 3,288 MW plus 550 MWh of standalone BESS. Since 31st March 2026 the Company has, through its subsidiaries, commissioned a further 2,297 MWh of BESS, taking total operational BESS capacity to 3,621 MWh at the end of July 2026, and added 8 MW of wind capacity from the ACME Eco Clean Energy Private Limited wind project, taking operational portfolio capacity to 2,990 MW as of 31st July 2026; PPAs of 600 MW were signed over the same period, lifting the PPA-signed portfolio to 3,880 MW. Technology-wise the contracted portfolio comprises 3,140 MW of solar, 150 MW of installed wind and 4,780 MW of FDRE and hybrid projects, with about 20 GWh of BESS. The majority of planned BESS capacity is linked to PPA-backed projects and will be connected to operational or near-term temporary GNA-ready substations, mitigating transmission connectivity risk and enabling early monetisation of cash flows, while commissioned BESS is being run on a short-term merchant basis using the existing transmission infrastructure of operational projects. Land and connectivity are secured ahead of execution, with over 15,000 acres secured across 11 states (3,000+ additional acres acquired since 31st March 2026) and roughly 10 GW of connectivity inventory available for upcoming bids. Execution is expected to scale by an additional ~1.5 GW in FY 2027, with a stated target of a 10 GW operational renewable portfolio and 25 GWh of BESS by 2030. Milestones include a pilot 15 MW solar project in Gujarat in 2011, 1 GW installed by 2017 across 10 states, over 2 GW by 2018, 3 GW commissioned by 2022, 3,380 MW of hybrid and FDRE projects secured in 2023-24 alongside a 1,200 MW ISTS project commissioned in Rajasthan and a first 150 MW wind project awarded by GUVNL in Gujarat, and diversification into BESS with Indian Railways' first 130 MW Round-the-Clock renewable tender secured in 2025.

- **One-offs / notes:** Other income (INR157 cr) is recurring SPV interest + DSRA interest (DSRA debt-funded, so finance cost offsets it — not a clean profit add). BESS contributed ~negligible revenue in Q4 (commissioned late-March); ~INR2.2 cr/day net realisation (>INR60 cr/month) is forward run-rate, not yet in FY26 P&L. Run-rate EBITDA incl. other income ~INR2,200 cr from operational fleet.
guidance (next 12 months / fy27):
- **FY27 commissioning target: ~1.5 GW of generation + ~10 GWh of BESS** (BESS ahead of generation).
- Of the 10 GWh: **~8.5 GWh on merchant basis, ~1.5 GWh in FDRE format** (Neemuch substation).
- Merchant BESS EBITDA margin guided **75-80%** (sell ~INR8, buy ~INR2, ~INR6 arbitrage).
- Under-construction PPA-signed portfolio commissioned by **FY28**.
- ~2,500 MW of ready substation connectivity (Fatehgarh-1 1,000+1,200 MW, Fatehgarh-2 1,000 MW, Bikaner-3) to transmit battery power.
order book & pipeline:
- Won 301 MWp FDRE with SECI during the quarter → UC portfolio 5.1 GW, total 8,071 MW (requires ~17 GWh BESS install).
- ~6.2 GW signed PPA (3.2 GW UC under construction + 1.8 GW recently won + ~850 MW older PPAs in discussion).
- Committed capex INR12,475 cr (INR6,445 cr incurred in FY26 + INR6,030 cr purchase orders).
- FY27 PPA conversion expected faster (single REIA = SECI); sector bids likely lower in count (~15-20 GW) but higher capex intensity due to FDRE/storage configuration.
segment / subsidiary:
- Generation SPVs upstream cash to ASHL (interest income at SPV level).
- 2.2 GW operational projects carry AA- stable credit rating.
- 550 MWh standalone Andhra BESS = pure leasing (NHPC offtake, VGF) — <1% of capex, IRR mid-high teens, zero date not yet started (trading-margin dispute on NHPC: 0.5% vs INR7 paisa).
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Merchant BESS arbitrage** is the key near-term optionality — battery charged from grid/curtailed power, sold at peak; PPA-agnostic, financed on merchant basis for flexibility.
- 654 MWh "merchant" BESS in UC slated to slot into an unsigned peak-power PPA (~INR6.28 tariff).
- Capex deferral lever: defer module purchase (~60% of solar capex, available just-in-time) until LTOA live → improves IRR, saves IDC.
margins & cost dynamics:
- BESS round-trip efficiency 88-90% (in line/better than expected).
- Weighted-avg cost of debt (operational) 8.4%; refinanced INR3,300 cr at ~150 bps lower; secured ~INR15,000 cr UC financing in FY26.
- DSO collapsed to ~14-15 days (from ~180 days in FY23-era) — structural, driven by 100% central offtake + cash discounts (pay in 10-30 days) + LPS scheme enforcement (Andhra/Telangana dues settled).
capex / expansion:
- FY26 capex incurred INR6,445 cr; total committed INR12,475 cr.
- Gross block +~INR3,460 cr YoY (~INR1,000-1,100 cr battery).
- Capital advances ~INR323 cr (10% on batteries w/ BG, 20% on turbines).
- BESS arriving monthly; commissioning at operational (brownfield) substations, not greenfield, to prepone revenue.
capital allocation:
- Prioritising early BESS deployment at existing substations to monetise spare transmission capacity.
- Disciplined capex deferral on solar modules where substations delayed (no penalty under CTU sync framework).
- Refinancing to lower interest cost; debt-covenant DSRA maintained.
risks & watch-items:
- **Other income / DSRA optics:** INR157 cr "other income" is debt-funded interest with offsetting finance cost — quality of reported PAT lower than headline.
- **Merchant arbitrage durability:** ~75-80% margins assume INR6 arbitrage persists; mgmt guides 4-5 yrs of elevated peak prices (INR9-10 thermal peak), but admits "anybody's guess." As ~200-300 GWh national BESS builds out, spread compresses.
- **Transmission/CTU delays:** ~6-month typical delay; only ~60% substations on time; revenue timing risk (mitigated by BESS preponement).
- **Curtailment:** small (~INR5-6 cr FY26 real curtailment); 2 Rajasthan state-grid projects exposed; rest CTU-protected.
- **Standalone BESS zero-date stuck** on NHPC trading-margin regulatory dispute.
- Supply-chain/geopolitical risk on battery cell imports.
management quality / tone: - Confident, granular, candid — quantified curtailment, named substation-by-substation timelines, openly flagged DSRA/other-income mechanics. CFO transition (Rajat Kumar Singh → Arun Chopra) handled smoothly. Strong command of regulatory nuance (MNRE/CERC/CTU/REIA). Tone bullish on BESS-led firming demand.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The MNRE clarification (BESS charged from conventional power under FDRE can sell merchant without buyer NOC until RE commissions) is the single biggest revenue-preponement enabler — ACME is exploiting energised brownfield substations to run batteries years before PPA COD.
- "Plain vanilla solar is the hardest to sell"; states now demand at least 1-2 hrs peak power → industry capex per MW rising even as headline GW bids fall (FDRE carries 1.5-2x solar behind battery).
- Deferring module capex (just-in-time, 60% of cost) is a structural IRR lever the whole industry uses under the no-penalty CTU sync regime.
- DSO of 14 days for an Indian renewable IPP is exceptional and reflects deliberate 100%-central-offtake portfolio construction (consciously avoided C&I/state-grid).

themes.title: Renewable IPP / FDRE firm-power & storage
themes.need: DISCOMs mandating firm/round-the-clock RE make BESS + pumped-hydro the bid differentiator, and in Q1FY27 storage demand ran ahead of supply. ADANIGREEN has 3.5 GWh of BESS installed (+1.9 GWh at Khavda this quarter), targets 10+ GWh this fiscal and 50 GWh by FY30 on a thumb-rule INR 25-30 lakh of EBITDA per MWh against ~INR 1.5cr/MWh of capex, and has contracted essentially all merchant/C&I capacity to sibling AESL on 25-year (solar/wind) and 15-year (battery) fixed-price PPAs targeting ~15-16% IRR - a pivot from merchant builder to fixed-return contracted IPP, with evacuation (not panels) named as the binding constraint. JSWENERGY added 873 MW in Q1 and ~1.1 GW since April - 36% of its 3 GW FY27 target already banked, Tidong Hydro commissioned four months early - and raised INR 10,150cr, taking net leverage 5.2x to 4.95x. On the equipment side SERVOTECH said its BESS pack capacity is fully booked ('we are not able to meet the demand') and committed to 2x capacity in 6 months, 3x by 21-Mar-2027 and 10x within 2 years. ACMESOLAR/KPIGREEN/SUZLON/INOXWIND attach storage to solar/wind; NTPC/NHPC/SJVN/TATAPOWER drive pumped-hydro and utility-scale storage.
themes.driver: BESS capacity commissioning against demand two independent managements (ADANIGREEN, SERVOTECH) say already exceeds supply; FDRE/peak-power tender awards; merchant DAM prices (JSWENERGY: INR 4.40 -> INR 5.10/unit, +16%) on +8.5% Q1 power demand.
